response.query: What are the top creative and quality trends in Humanities, Literature, and Arts related to language hierarchy, affective harms, resistance, decoloniality, and education policies, based on our current research on English-in-education in low-SES Bangladeshi schools?
response.answer: Current trends emphasize decoloniality, resistance to language hierarchy, and innovative multilingual education policies to combat affective harms in low-SES contexts. Creative approaches focus on fostering critical-affective pedagogy and multilingualism for cultural and cognitive benefits. Research highlights the importance of inclusive, equitable language education practices.

results.title: A creative approach to fighting the decline of language learning in schools | by Oxford Humanities | Innovating in the Humanities | Medium
results.content: A series profiling some of the research and researchers in Oxford’s Humanities Division, in collaboration with external partners, who are developing new insights, ideas and innovations. Professor Katrin Kohl and Professor Neil Kenny have dedicated their careers to modern languages, but their academic research interests, spanning early modern French literature and the language and literature of modern Germany, have also operated as springboards for policy and engagement work. By collaborating with schools, teachers, and policymakers, both are actively working to ensure that future generations can also enjoy an education in modern languages. Professor Kenny, who is Lead Fellow for Languages at the British Academy, acts as a key link between education and modern language researchers and policymakers. In 2019, Professor Kenny and his colleagues at the British Academy, together with the three other national academies, published ‘Languages in the UK: a call for action’, calling for the government to develop a national languages strategy. Professor Kohl, too, has worked on developing the school languages curriculum, and has collaborated with academics, teachers, schools and policymakers to ensure that the most important voices in the debate are heard. Alongside her policy work, Professor Kohl has engaged with teachers and students to encourage German uptake in schools. This approach bore fruit in the interdisciplinary research project “Creative Multilingualism” (funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council, 2016–2020), led by Professor Kohl and involving colleagues in modern languages, linguistics, English, media studies, education, anthropology and biology from six universities. “We researched the value of language diversity for creative thinking and expression,” says Professor Kohl. But it’s all worth it for the ones that work,” Professor Kenny says. A series profiling some of the research and researchers in Oxford’s Humanities Division, in collaboration with external partners, who are developing new insights, ideas and innovations. ## More from Oxford Humanities and Innovating in the Humanities. ### Professor Abigail Williams, Associate Head of Research and Innovation for the Humanities at Oxford University, introduces the series. ### Professor Aditi Lahiri has developed a new technology with exciting possibilities for speech, language learning, healthcare, and more.

Creative Writing is a dynamic and high-achieving subject area in the School, whose members produce award-winning creative work as well as innovative practice-led research. * English Literature, Language and Linguistics. ## Strong tradition of creative and critical dialogue. Our poets, prose writers, scriptwriters, and film-makers not only maintain impressive levels of creative output, but also contribute to the strong tradition of creative and critical dialogue in the School, which began in 1967 with the appointment of the first Literary Fellow, Tony Harrison. Research in film and screenwriting takes place across several Schools in the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences. We produce prize-winning scholarly research and creative writing for stage, screen and radio. Our research cluster produces award-winning writing across the novel, the short story, the memoir, and creative non-fiction. Creative Writing and Literature colleagues work together to explore the interface between a series of academic, civic, and artistic endeavours through practice-led research. * the pedagogy of creative writing. The NCLA's primary aim is to contribute to the cultural life of the North East of England through the provision of readings, events, education, publications, and creative projects. The School has an impressive publishing partnership with Bloodaxe, which started by sponsoring the Newcastle/Bloodaxe Poetry Lectures as a book series, and has produced a series of anthologies including *The Poetry Cure* and *Out of Bounds*. #### Children's Literature.
